624.title: Holy, holy, holy (Apocalypse 4)
624.hook: around the throne the living creatures never stop singing
624.howItsDone: At every Mass, at the end of the Preface, the priest invites the people to join the angels and saints, and all sing or say the Sanctus, Holy, Holy, Holy, drawn from Isaiah 6 and Apocalypse 4.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lantern at an overgrown door. Your line was I stand and knock.

A door again, but this time it opens the other way. John writes: "behold a door was opened in heaven." A voice like a trumpet says, come up here. Suddenly John isn't looking at seven small churches in Asia anymore. Until now the book has kept its eyes on earth; here the camera swings up, through a doorway into the center of everything. And what John sees first isn't a battle, or a beast, or a timeline. It's worship.
screen: `A DOOR OPENED IN HEAVEN.` → `COME UP HITHER.` → `THE CENTER OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: John reaches for words. The one on the throne looks like jasper and sardine stone. A rainbow like emerald circles the throne. Lightning, thunder, seven burning lamps, and before it a sea of glass like crystal. Around it sit twenty-four elders in white, with gold crowns. Close around the throne, four living creatures: one like a lion, one like a calf, one with a man's face, one like a flying eagle, each with six wings and covered with eyes. Then the sound, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they rested not day and night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come." Rested not: the song never stops. John's readers would have heard an echo. Long before, in the temple, the prophet Isaiah saw the seraphim crying to each other: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." Holy is often explained as set apart, other, nothing like us; saying it three times piles it as high as the words will go. Then the elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne. Every honor they have, they give back. Catholics know this song. At every Mass, at the end of the Preface, the priest speaks of joining the angels and saints in their hymn, and the people sing the Sanctus: holy, holy, holy. The Church says the Mass on earth joins the worship John saw through that open door. Later Christian tradition made the four creatures symbols of the four Gospel writers: Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the calf, John the eagle.
screen: `JASPER, EMERALD, A SEA OF GLASS.` · `FOUR LIVING CREATURES.` · `ISAIAH HEARD IT TOO.` · `THE SANCTUS AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, LORD GOD ALMIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Picture what John saw: the open door, the rainbow, the sea of glass, the creatures with their wings, the elders laying down their crowns, and let it be bright and loud. Then imagine the song has been going on the whole time, through every ordinary minute of your day. If you pray, join it softly, holy, holy, holy, once on each out-breath; if not, just listen in your mind to a song that never rests.
Holy. Set apart, wholly other. Sung three times by the creatures around the throne, and by the people at every Mass. Today's word.
Your line: they rest not. The song was going before you arrived. That's day six hundred twenty-four.

625.title: The Lamb that was slain (Apocalypse 5)
625.hook: the Mass joins this heavenly liturgy (CCC 1090)
625.howItsDone: At every Mass, while the host is broken, the people sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, three times, and the priest then shows the host with the words of John the Baptist, Behold the Lamb of God; the Church teaches that the earthly liturgy shares in the heavenly one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the door opened in heaven, and holy, holy, holy. Your line was they rest not.

In Handel's Messiah, audiences stand for the Hallelujah chorus, but it isn't the ending. The Hallelujah closes the second part. The whole work ends later, with a slower, larger chorus and then an Amen that goes on and on, voices climbing over each other. Its words, worthy is the Lamb that was slain, come from the fifth chapter of the Apocalypse, where they're sung in heaven, by a choir far bigger than any concert hall could hold.
screen: `NOT THE HALLELUJAH.` → `THE LAST CHORUS OF MESSIAH.` → `WORTHY IS THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Chapter five begins with a problem. In the right hand of the one on the throne is a scroll, written inside and out, sealed with seven seals. A strong angel calls out: who is worthy to open it? No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth can. John weeps much, he says. Then an elder tells him: weep not; the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the root of David, has won, and can open the scroll. John turns to look for a lion, and sees a Lamb. Standing, yet looking as though it had been slain. Told a lion, he sees a lamb with its wounds still showing. That's the whole book in one image: the power that wins is a love that was killed and is alive. John's Greek word is arnion, which can mean a little lamb. The Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven erupts. The creatures and the elders fall down with harps and bowls of incense, which the text says are the prayers of the saints. Thousands upon thousands of angels sing, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lamb that was slain is worthy to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and benediction." Then every creature, in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, joins in. Catholics hear this at Mass. As the host is broken before Communion, the people sing or say the Lamb of God, and the priest holds up the host and says, behold the Lamb of God. The Catechism says the liturgy on earth already shares in this heavenly one.
screen: `A SCROLL NO ONE CAN OPEN.` · `TOLD A LION, JOHN SEES A LAMB.` · `THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS.` · `THE LAMB OF GOD AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THE LAMB THAT WAS SLAIN IS WORTHY.`

segments.voice: Picture the throne, the scroll, the Lamb standing with its wounds showing, and every creature everywhere singing, and let your own small voice be one of them. If you don't pray, just picture the Lamb, and notice what it means that the winner has wounds.

Your line: worthy is the lamb. Told a lion, John saw a lamb. See you tomorrow.

626.title: A great multitude (Apocalypse 7:9–17)
626.hook: from all nations, tribes, peoples and tongues; read on All Saints
626.tomorrow: a woman clothed with the sun
626.howItsDone: On the Solemnity of All Saints, November 1, Catholics hear Apocalypse 7 at Mass and honor all the saints, known and unknown; the next day, All Souls, they pray for all the faithful departed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arnion: the Lamb standing with its wounds still showing. Your line was worthy is the lamb.

On the first of November, the Church celebrates All Saints. Not one saint: all of them. The famous ones with statues, and the ones nobody ever canonized: the grandmother who prayed the rosary on the bus, the farmer who never missed Sunday, the nurse who held hands on night shifts. Names no calendar has room for. The first reading at Mass that day comes from Apocalypse seven. It begins with a number, and then John looks up and sees something no number can hold.
screen: `THE FIRST OF NOVEMBER.` → `SAINTS NO CALENDAR CAN HOLD.` → `A NUMBER, THEN A CROWD.`

segments.voice: First John hears a number: a hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel. Twelve times twelve, times a thousand: Catholic interpreters read it as a symbol of the whole people of God, complete. Then, just as he heard of a lion and saw a lamb, he hears a number and sees a crowd. In the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." Every accent and alphabet on earth, standing together. Palms in their hands, a sign of victory, like the crowd that waved branches when Jesus rode into Jerusalem. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. Then an elder asks John: who are these in white, and where did they come from? John, overwhelmed, says simply, "My lord, thou knowest." The elder tells him: "These are they who are come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and have made them white in the blood of the Lamb." Robes washed in blood come out white. These aren't people who avoided suffering; they came through it. And the chapter ends with a promise for them: no more hunger, no more thirst, no burning sun. The Lamb will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water. On All Saints, Catholics remember that this crowd includes people they knew.
screen: `A NUMBER: 144,000.` · `A CROWD NO MAN COULD NUMBER.` · `MY LORD, THOU KNOWEST.` · `WASHED WHITE IN THE BLOOD OF THE LAMB.` · then, large: `ALL NATIONS, AND TRIBES, AND PEOPLES, AND TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Imagine a huge open space before a throne, filling with people from every continent: old women in headscarves, teenagers, farmers, a child holding a palm branch, a man in a wheelchair, languages you don't know. Let it fill until you can't see the edges, then look for someone you knew who has died, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, in white, holding a palm. If you pray, you can ask them to pray for you; if not, just let yourself see them there.

627.title: A woman clothed with the sun (Apocalypse 12)
627.hook: the moon under her feet and twelve stars; read on the Assumption as Mary and the Church
627.howItsDone: Catholics hear Apocalypse 12 on the Solemnity of the Assumption, August 15, and Marian art, especially images of the Immaculate Conception, often shows Mary with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great multitude in white, palms in their hands. Your line was every tongue.

Nearly six hundred years before Christ, Babylon's army burned the temple in Jerusalem. After that, the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, is never seen again in the Bible's history. One old story, in Second Maccabees, says the prophet Jeremiah hid it in a cave on a mountain until God gathers his people again. Then, at the very end of Apocalypse eleven, John sees God's temple in heaven open, and there it is: the ark. The very next thing he sees isn't a chest at all. It's a woman.
screen: `THE ARK, LOST WITH THE TEMPLE.` → `SEEN AGAIN IN HEAVEN.` → `THEN, A WOMAN.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." She's about to give birth, crying out in pain. Then a second sign: a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, waiting to devour the child as soon as it's born. The child, a son who will rule all the nations, is born and caught up to God and to his throne. The woman flees into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared for her. Then war breaks out in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon, and the dragon is thrown down. The text names him: that old serpent, the devil. That reaches back to Genesis, where God tells the serpent there will be enmity between him and the woman, between his seed and hers. Who is the woman? Catholic tradition doesn't pick just one answer. She is Mary, who bore the child who rules the nations; the Church reads this passage on the feast of the Assumption, in August. She is also the Church, the people of God, who bring Christ into the world in pain and are kept safe in the wilderness. Many readers also see Israel in her twelve stars, the twelve tribes. The symbols carry more than one meaning at once. And remember how the scene began: with the ark of the covenant. Catholic tradition has long called Mary the ark of the new covenant, the one who carried God within her.

If you pray, you can ask Mary to pray for you; if not, just stay with the sky.

628.title: Babylon falls (Apocalypse 18)
628.hook: the merchants weep over a city built on luxury
628.howItsDone: Catholic social teaching warns against consumerism and insists that people are never merchandise; Catholics practice simplicity through fasting and almsgiving, especially in Lent, and support fair labor and the fight against human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman with the moon under her feet. Your line was clothed with the sun.

Open a shopping app and scroll. Gold jewelry. Silk scarves. Perfume. Fine wine. Imported spices. Everything delivered to your door, from somewhere you'll never see, made by people you'll never meet. Now read chapter eighteen of the Apocalypse, and you'll find almost the same list: gold, silver, pearls, silk, scarlet, ivory, cinnamon, perfume, wine, oil, fine flour, cattle, horses, chariots. It's the shipping manifest of that great city, Babylon. And everyone who traded in it is standing at a distance, crying, because the city is gone.
screen: `SCROLLING A SHOPPING APP.` → `THE SAME LIST, IN THE APOCALYPSE.` → `THE CITY IS GONE.`

segments.voice: In the Apocalypse, Babylon is a code name, and a long line of readers have taken it as Rome: chapter seventeen speaks of seven mountains, and Rome was rich, powerful, and hard on those who wouldn't bow. The first letter of Peter seems to use the same code, sending greetings from the church in Babylon. In chapter eighteen an angel lights up the earth with his glory and cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen." Then a voice from heaven: "Go out from her, my people; that you be not partakers of her sins." Then three groups of mourners: kings who lived in luxury with her, merchants who got rich off her, sailors who carried her cargo. They stand far off, afraid, saying the same thing: in one hour her judgment came; in one hour her riches were laid waste. Three times the text says it. Listen to the list to the very end. After the horses and chariots, the last items are bodies and human souls. People, bought and sold like the cinnamon. That's what the luxury was standing on. Then an angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea: like that, Babylon will be thrown down and found no more. No more music in her streets, no more lamps, no more bride and bridegroom. The chapter isn't against beauty or trade. It's about a whole way of life that forgot people were not merchandise, and how fast it can vanish. Catholic social teaching makes a similar warning.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last few things you bought or almost bought, and pick one you didn't really need, the one that was more about the scroll than the need; imagine not buying it, and notice if anything in you protests. Then think about who made the things you do buy: the hands, the fields, the factories, the drivers. If you pray, pray for them; if not, just hold them in mind for a moment, people, not merchandise.

629.title: The supper of the Lamb (Apocalypse 19:6–9)
629.hook: blessed are they that are called: echoed at every Mass
629.howItsDone: Before Communion at every Mass, the priest shows the host and says Behold the Lamb of God, adding that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed; the people respond with the centurion's words, Lord, I am not worthy, and the Church teaches that the Eucharist anticipates the wedding feast of the Lamb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babylon fell in one hour, and the merchants wept. Your line was what doesn't last.

Alleluia is sung at Mass all year, except in Lent. It's in hymns, on Easter cards, in the names of choirs. Now look for it in the Apocalypse: in chapter nineteen it comes four times, close together. Right after Babylon falls, the noise of the merchants weeping is drowned out by another sound. John hears what sounds like a great crowd, like many waters, like great thunders, shouting alleluia. Then they say why. There's going to be a wedding.
screen: `ALLELUIA, ALL YEAR LONG.` → `FOUR TIMES IN APOCALYPSE NINETEEN.` → `THERE'S GOING TO BE A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: The crowd sings that the Lord God Almighty reigns. Let us be glad and rejoice, they say, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready. She's given fine linen to wear, bright and clean, and the text explains the linen: it's the good deeds of the saints. So the bride is the Church, God's people, dressed in the love they've lived. Babylon was dressed in purple and scarlet, bought and sold. The bride is dressed in deeds. Then an angel tells John to write something down, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb." These are the true words of God, the angel adds. Again and again in the Bible, God's love for his people is pictured as a marriage, from the prophets to Jesus's parable of the wedding feast. Here that picture becomes a feast. Catholics hear it at every Mass. Just before Communion, the priest holds up the host and says, behold the Lamb of God, and then that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed. In Latin: beati qui ad cenam Agni vocati sunt. The people answer with the words of a centurion from Matthew's Gospel, as the Douay-Rheims gives them: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word. Called, and not worthy, and coming anyway. The Church teaches that every Mass is a foretaste of this wedding feast.

630.title: All things new (Apocalypse 21:1–5)
630.hook: God shall wipe away every tear
630.carry: behold, I make all things new
630.howItsDone: Apocalypse 21 is among the readings families may choose for a Catholic funeral Mass, and the Church teaches that at the end of time the whole universe will be renewed, with God dwelling among his people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alleluia, a wedding, and cenam Agni, the supper of the Lamb. Your line was called to the supper.

A kid falls off a bike. Scraped knee, gravel in the palm, a howl you can hear three houses away. A parent comes running and, before the bandage, before anything, takes the child's face in both hands and wipes the tears off with a thumb. You have to be very close to do it. Near the end of the Apocalypse, after the dragon and the beasts and Babylon, John says God will do exactly that.
screen: `A SCRAPED KNEE ON THE SIDEWALK.` → `A THUMB ACROSS A WET CHEEK.` → `GOD WILL DO EXACTLY THAT.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth." And the sea is no more. Some readers hear the sea as a picture of chaos, and John, remember, was on an island, cut off by water. Then: "And I John saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." Notice the direction. The city comes down. The story doesn't end with people escaping earth; it ends with heaven coming to earth. A great voice says: "Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them." The Greek word behind tabernacle means a tent: God pitching his tent among his people, the same image John's Gospel uses when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Catholics also call the place in church where the Eucharist is kept the tabernacle. Then: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more, for the former things are passed away." Not prevent the tears: wipe them. They were real. Then the one on the throne speaks: "Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things, a replacement world with the old one thrown out. All things, made new. The Catechism teaches that the universe itself will be renewed, not discarded. The Church offers this among the readings at funerals, to families whose tears haven't been wiped yet.

If there's a sorrow of your own, let someone do the same for you; you can even touch your own cheek with your thumb. If you pray, rest in the promise, God shall wipe away all tears; if not, just let the gentleness stay.
